simpleVersion: King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya what his sons and the Pandavas did after gathering on the sacred battlefield of Kurukshetra.
explanation: King Dhritarashtra asks Sanjaya to report what is happening on the holy plain of Kurukshetra. Both his own sons and the sons of Pandu have gathered there, ready for battle. He wants to know what they did once they assembled.

source.sanskrit:
धृतराष्ट्र उवाच

धर्मक्षेत्रे कुरुक्षेत्रे समवेता युयुत्सवः।

मामकाः पाण्डवाश्चैव किमकुर्वत सञ्जय।।1.1।।
source.transliteration:
dhṛitarāśhtra uvācha
dharma-kṣhetre kuru-kṣhetre samavetā yuyutsavaḥ
māmakāḥ pāṇḍavāśhchaiva kimakurvata sañjaya
source.translation: Dhritarashtra said, "What did my people and the sons of Pandu do when they had assembled together, eager for battle, on the holy plain of Kurukshetra, O Sanjaya?"

simpleVersion: Sanjaya describes how King Duryodhana observed the organized Pandava army and went to talk to his teacher, Drona.
explanation: Sanjaya reports what is happening on the battlefield. King Duryodhana sees that the opposing Pandava army is fully prepared and arranged for battle. Seeing this, he walks over to speak with his teacher, Drona.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

दृष्ट्वा तु पाण्डवानीकं व्यूढं दुर्योधनस्तदा।

आचार्यमुपसङ्गम्य राजा वचनमब्रवीत्।।1.2।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
dṛiṣhṭvā tu pāṇḍavānīkaṁ vyūḍhaṁ duryodhanastadā
āchāryamupasaṅgamya rājā vachanamabravīt
source.translation: Sanjaya said: Having seen the army of the Pandavas drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher, Drona, and spoke these words.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana points out the large Pandava army to his teacher, noting it was organized by his teacher's talented student.
explanation: In this verse, Duryodhana speaks to his teacher, Drona. He asks him to look at the massive army gathered by the Pandavas. He highlights that this army was arranged by the son of Drupada, who is Drona's own skilled student.

source.sanskrit:
पश्यैतां पाण्डुपुत्राणामाचार्य महतीं चमूम्।

व्यूढां द्रुपदपुत्रेण तव शिष्येण धीमता।।1.3।।
source.transliteration:
paśhyaitāṁ pāṇḍu-putrāṇām āchārya mahatīṁ chamūm
vyūḍhāṁ drupada-putreṇa tava śhiṣhyeṇa dhīmatā
source.translation: Behold, O Teacher! This mighty army of the sons of Pandu, arrayed by the son of Drupada, thy wise disciple.

simpleVersion: This verse lists great archers and heroic warriors in the army who are as powerful in battle as Bhima and Arjuna.
explanation: This verse names several powerful heroes and archers present on the battlefield. It highlights skilled warriors like Yuyudhana, Virata, and Drupada, comparing their strength in battle to famous fighters like Bhima and Arjuna.

source.sanskrit:
अत्र शूरा महेष्वासा भीमार्जुनसमा युधि।

युयुधानो विराटश्च द्रुपदश्च महारथः।।1.4।।
source.transliteration:
atra śhūrā maheṣhvāsā bhīmārjuna-samā yudhi
yuyudhāno virāṭaśhcha drupadaśhcha mahā-rathaḥ
source.translation: Here are heroes, mighty archers, equal in battle to Bhima and Arjuna, Yuyudhana (Satyaki), Virata, and Drupada—all mighty warriors.

simpleVersion: This verse names several heroic kings and warriors present on the battlefield, describing them as the best of men.
explanation: This verse lists key warriors standing on the battlefield. It names Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the powerful king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya. These individuals are praised as outstanding and brave leaders among men.

source.sanskrit:
धृष्टकेतुश्चेकितानः काशिराजश्च वीर्यवान्।

पुरुजित्कुन्तिभोजश्च शैब्यश्च नरपुङ्गवः।।1.5।।
source.transliteration:
dhṛiṣhṭaketuśhchekitānaḥ kāśhirājaśhcha vīryavān
purujit kuntibhojaśhcha śhaibyaśhcha nara-puṅgavaḥ
yudhāmanyuśhcha vikrānta uttamaujāśhcha vīryavān
source.translation: Dhrishtaketu, Chekitana, the valiant king of Kasi, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Saibya—the best of men.

simpleVersion: This verse lists powerful warriors in the army, including Yudhamanyu, Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and the sons of Draupadi, calling them all great heroes.
explanation: Duryodhana continues naming the key fighters on the opposing side. He highlights strong warriors like Yudhamanyu, brave Uttamaujas, Abhimanyu, and Draupadi’s sons. He recognizes that all of them are elite warriors.

source.sanskrit:
युधामन्युश्च विक्रान्त उत्तमौजाश्च वीर्यवान्।

सौभद्रो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्व एव महारथाः।।1.6।।
source.transliteration: saubhadro draupadeyāśhcha sarva eva mahā-rathāḥ
source.translation: The strong Yudhamanyu and the brave Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadra (Abhimanyu, the son of Subhadra and Arjuna), and the sons of Draupadi, all of them great charioteers (great heroes)."

simpleVersion: Duryodhana speaks to his teacher and offers to list the key commanders leading their army.
explanation: Duryodhana addresses his teacher, calling him the best among the twice-born. He wants to point out the most distinguished leaders commanding their army so his teacher is fully informed.

source.sanskrit:
अस्माकं तु विशिष्टा ये तान्निबोध द्विजोत्तम।

नायका मम सैन्यस्य संज्ञार्थं तान्ब्रवीमि ते।।1.7।।
source.transliteration:
asmākaṁ tu viśhiṣhṭā ye tānnibodha dwijottama
nāyakā mama sainyasya sanjñārthaṁ tānbravīmi te
source.translation: Know also, O best among the twice-born! the names of those who are the most distinguished amongst ourselves, the leaders of my army; these I name to you for your information.

simpleVersion: This verse names major victorious warriors—including Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava—who are fully prepared for battle.
explanation: In this verse, specific powerful military leaders ready for combat are named. These fighters include Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava. They are all described as victorious warriors who are assembled and prepared to fight.

source.sanskrit:
भवान्भीष्मश्च कर्णश्च कृपश्च समितिञ्जयः।

अश्वत्थामा विकर्णश्च सौमदत्तिस्तथैव च।।1.8।।
source.transliteration:
bhavānbhīṣhmaśhcha karṇaśhcha kṛipaśhcha samitiñjayaḥ
aśhvatthāmā vikarṇaśhcha saumadattis tathaiva cha
source.translation: "Thou thyself, Bhishma, Karna, Kripa, the victorious in war, Asvatthama, Vikarna, and Bhurisrava, the son of Somadatta—all these are ready for battle."

simpleVersion: Duryodhana points out that many other skilled heroes, armed with various weapons, are ready to lay down their lives for him.
explanation: Duryodhana is describing the rest of his army to Drona. He points out that there are many brave warriors who are highly trained in battle and equipped with many types of weapons. Crucially, these fighters are willing to risk and give up their lives for his cause.

source.sanskrit:
अन्ये च बहवः शूरा मदर्थे त्यक्तजीविताः।

नानाशस्त्रप्रहरणाः सर्वे युद्धविशारदाः।।1.9।।
source.transliteration:
anye cha bahavaḥ śhūrā madarthe tyaktajīvitāḥ
nānā-śhastra-praharaṇāḥ sarve yuddha-viśhāradāḥ
source.translation: And also many other heroes, ready to give up their lives for my sake, armed with various weapons and missiles, all well-skilled in battle.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana states that his army, protected by Bhishma, is insufficient, while the opposing army, led by Bhima, is sufficient.
explanation: In this verse, Duryodhana compares the strength of the two opposing forces. He assesses his own army, commanded by Bhishma, as inadequate. In contrast, he considers the enemy army, guarded by Bhima, to be fully sufficient.

source.sanskrit:
अपर्याप्तं तदस्माकं बलं भीष्माभिरक्षितम्।

पर्याप्तं त्विदमेतेषां बलं भीमाभिरक्षितम्।।1.10।।
source.transliteration:
aparyāptaṁ tadasmākaṁ balaṁ bhīṣhmābhirakṣhitam
paryāptaṁ tvidameteṣhāṁ balaṁ bhīmābhirakṣhitam
source.translation: Our army, marshalled by Bhishma, is insufficient, whereas theirs, marshalled by Bhima, is sufficient.

simpleVersion: Duryodhana orders every warrior to hold their position and focus above all on protecting Bhishma.
explanation: Continuing his address to Drona, Duryodhana commands all his warriors to take their assigned positions across the army's divisions. Above everything else, he insists they concentrate on protecting Bhishma, their commander-in-chief.

source.sanskrit:
अयनेषु च सर्वेषु यथाभागमवस्थिताः।

भीष्ममेवाभिरक्षन्तु भवन्तः सर्व एव हि।।1.11।।
source.transliteration:
ayaneṣhu cha sarveṣhu yathā-bhāgamavasthitāḥ
bhīṣhmamevābhirakṣhantu bhavantaḥ sarva eva hi
source.translation: Therefore, do all of you, stationed in your respective positions in the several divisions of the army, protect Bhishma alone.

simpleVersion: Bhishma, the eldest Kaurava, roars like a lion and blows his conch to lift Duryodhana's spirits.
explanation: Sensing his grandson's anxiety, Bhishma responds with a display of confidence. He roars like a lion and sounds his conch loudly, a traditional signal marking readiness for war, meant to cheer Duryodhana.

source.sanskrit:
तस्य संजनयन्हर्षं कुरुवृद्धः पितामहः।

सिंहनादं विनद्योच्चैः शङ्खं दध्मौ प्रतापवान्।।1.12।।
source.transliteration:
tasya sañjanayan harṣhaṁ kuru-vṛiddhaḥ pitāmahaḥ
siṁha-nādaṁ vinadyochchaiḥ śhaṅkhaṁ dadhmau pratāpavān
source.translation: His glorious grandsire, the oldest of the Kauravas, roared like a lion to cheer Duryodhana and blew his conch.

simpleVersion: Following Bhishma's conch, a deafening wave of conches, drums, and horns erupts across the Kaurava army.
explanation: Bhishma's conch sets off a chain reaction. Conches, kettledrums, tabors, and horns suddenly sound together from the Kaurava side, producing an overwhelming wall of noise that signals the army is ready for war.

source.sanskrit:
ततः शङ्खाश्च भेर्यश्च पणवानकगोमुखाः।

सहसैवाभ्यहन्यन्त स शब्दस्तुमुलोऽभवत्।।1.13।।
source.transliteration:
tataḥ śhaṅkhāśhcha bheryaśhcha paṇavānaka-gomukhāḥ
sahasaivābhyahanyanta sa śhabdastumulo ’bhavat
source.translation: Then, suddenly, conches, kettledrums, tabors, drums, and cow horns blared forth from the Kaurava side, and the sound was tremendous.

simpleVersion: Seated in their grand chariot pulled by white horses, Krishna and Arjuna answer by blowing their own divine conches.
explanation: On the other side of the battlefield, Krishna and Arjuna, riding together in a magnificent chariot drawn by white horses, respond to the Kaurava challenge. They sound their celestial conches to show the Pandavas are ready as well.

source.sanskrit:
ततः श्वेतैर्हयैर्युक्ते महति स्यन्दने स्थितौ।

माधवः पाण्डवश्चैव दिव्यौ शङ्खौ प्रदध्मतुः।।1.14।।
source.transliteration:
tataḥ śhvetairhayairyukte mahati syandane sthitau
mādhavaḥ pāṇḍavaśhchaiva divyau śhaṅkhau pradadhmatuḥ
source.translation: Then, Madhava (Krishna) and the son of Pandu (Arjuna), seated in the magnificent chariot yoked with white horses, blew divine conches.

simpleVersion: Krishna blows the conch Panchajanya, Arjuna blows Devadatta, and mighty Bhima blows the great conch Paundra.
explanation: This verse names the specific conches sounded by three key Pandava figures. Krishna sounds the Panchajanya, Arjuna the Devadatta, and Bhima, famed for his fearsome feats, sounds the massive Paundra.

source.sanskrit:
पाञ्चजन्यं हृषीकेशो देवदत्तं धनंजयः।

पौण्ड्रं दध्मौ महाशङ्खं भीमकर्मा वृकोदरः।।1.15।।
source.transliteration:
pāñchajanyaṁ hṛiṣhīkeśho devadattaṁ dhanañjayaḥ
pauṇḍraṁ dadhmau mahā-śhaṅkhaṁ bhīma-karmā vṛikodaraḥ
source.translation: Hrishikesha blew the Panchajanya, Arjuna blew the Devadatta, and Bhima, the wolf-bellied doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Paundra.

simpleVersion: King Yudhishthira blows the Anantavijaya conch, while his brothers Nakula and Sahadeva blow the Sughosha and Manipushpaka.
explanation: The list of Pandava conches continues. Yudhishthira, the eldest brother, sounds the Anantavijaya, while the twins Nakula and Sahadeva sound the Sughosha and Manipushpaka.

source.sanskrit:
अनन्तविजयं राजा कुन्तीपुत्रो युधिष्ठिरः।

नकुलः सहदेवश्च सुघोषमणिपुष्पकौ।।1.16।।
source.transliteration:
anantavijayaṁ rājā kuntī-putro yudhiṣhṭhiraḥ
nakulaḥ sahadevaśhcha sughoṣha-maṇipuṣhpakau
source.translation: King Yudhishthira, the son of Kunti, blew the Anantavijaya; Nakula and Sahadeva blew the Sughosha and the Manipushpaka.

simpleVersion: Other great warriors — the king of Kasi, Sikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the unconquered Satyaki — also sound their conches.
explanation: The roll call continues. Skilled fighters including the archer-king of Kasi, the mighty Sikhandi, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and the undefeated Satyaki all join in sounding their conches for battle.

source.sanskrit:
काश्यश्च परमेष्वासः शिखण्डी च महारथः।

धृष्टद्युम्नो विराटश्च सात्यकिश्चापराजितः।।1.17।।
source.transliteration:
kāśhyaśhcha parameṣhvāsaḥ śhikhaṇḍī cha mahā-rathaḥ
dhṛiṣhṭadyumno virāṭaśhcha sātyakiśh chāparājitaḥ
source.translation: The king of Kasi, an excellent archer, Sikhandi, the mighty car-warrior, Dhrishtadyumna, Virata, and Satyaki, the unconquered.

simpleVersion: Drupada, Draupadi's sons, and the mighty-armed Abhimanyu each blow their own conches separately.
explanation: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Drupada, the five sons of Draupadi, and Abhimanyu, son of Subhadra, each sound their individual conches, completing the roll call of Pandava warriors joining the call to battle.

source.sanskrit:
द्रुपदो द्रौपदेयाश्च सर्वशः पृथिवीपते।

सौभद्रश्च महाबाहुः शङ्खान्दध्मुः पृथक्पृथक्।।1.18।।
source.transliteration:
drupado draupadeyāśhcha sarvaśhaḥ pṛithivī-pate
saubhadraśhcha mahā-bāhuḥ śhaṅkhāndadhmuḥ pṛithak pṛithak
source.translation: Drupada and the sons of Draupadi, O Lord of the Earth, and the son of Subhadra, the mighty-armed, blew their conches each separately.

simpleVersion: The combined roar of Pandava conches is so overwhelming it shakes the hearts of Dhritarashtra's warriors and echoes through the sky and earth.
explanation: The noise unleashed by the Pandava side is described as thunderous, reverberating across heaven and earth. Its intensity strikes fear into the hearts of the Kaurava warriors, foreshadowing the weight of the coming battle.

source.sanskrit:
स घोषो धार्तराष्ट्राणां हृदयानि व्यदारयत्।

नभश्च पृथिवीं चैव तुमुलो व्यनुनादयन्।।1.19।।
source.transliteration:
sa ghoṣho dhārtarāṣhṭrāṇāṁ hṛidayāni vyadārayat
nabhaśhcha pṛithivīṁ chaiva tumulo nunādayan
source.translation: The tumultuous sound rent the hearts of Dhritarashtra's party, reverberating through both heaven and earth.

simpleVersion: As battle is about to begin, Arjuna raises his bow and turns to speak to Krishna, watching the enemy ranks standing ready.
explanation: With weapons about to clash, Arjuna, whose chariot flag bears a monkey emblem, looks at the Kaurava forces arrayed for war. He lifts his bow and turns to Krishna, about to make a request before the fighting starts.

source.sanskrit:
अथ व्यवस्थितान् दृष्ट्वा धार्तराष्ट्रान्कपिध्वजः।

प्रवृत्ते शस्त्रसंपाते धनुरुद्यम्य पाण्डवः।।1.20।।
source.transliteration:
atha vyavasthitān dṛiṣhṭvā dhārtarāṣhṭrān kapi-dhwajaḥ
pravṛitte śhastra-sampāte dhanurudyamya pāṇḍavaḥ
source.translation: Then, seeing the people of Dhritarashtra's party standing arrayed and the discharge of weapons about to begin, Arjuna, the son of Pandu whose ensign was a monkey, took up his bow and said the following to Krishna, O Lord of the Earth.

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks Krishna to drive his chariot to the middle, right between the two armies.
explanation: Addressing Krishna as Achyuta, 'the infallible one,' Arjuna makes his first request before the battle: to position his chariot exactly between the two opposing armies, so he can see who he will be facing.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

हृषीकेशं तदा वाक्यमिदमाह महीपते।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये रथं स्थापय मेऽच्युत।।1.21।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
senayor ubhayor madhye rathaṁ sthāpaya me ’chyuta
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, place my chariot in the middle between the two armies."

simpleVersion: He wants to see exactly who has gathered here, ready to fight, before the battle truly begins.
explanation: Arjuna continues his request to Krishna, explaining his reason: he wants a clear view of everyone who has assembled for battle, so he knows precisely who he will face once the fighting starts.

source.sanskrit:
यावदेतान्निरीक्षेऽहं योद्धुकामानवस्थितान्।

कैर्मया सह योद्धव्यमस्मिन्रणसमुद्यमे।।1.22।।
source.transliteration:
yāvadetān nirīkṣhe ’haṁ yoddhu-kāmān avasthitān
kairmayā saha yoddhavyam asmin raṇa-samudyame
source.translation: ...so that I may behold those who stand here, desirous to fight, and know with whom I must fight when the battle is about to commence.

simpleVersion: Arjuna wants to see which warriors have come to fight for Duryodhana, whom he calls evil-minded.
explanation: Arjuna clarifies further: he wants to observe the fighters who have gathered specifically to please Duryodhana, whom he openly calls evil-minded, before the battle begins.

source.sanskrit:
योत्स्यमानानवेक्षेऽहं य एतेऽत्र समागताः।

धार्तराष्ट्रस्य दुर्बुद्धेर्युद्धे प्रियचिकीर्षवः।।1.23।।
source.transliteration:
yotsyamānān avekṣhe ’haṁ ya ete ’tra samāgatāḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrasya durbuddher yuddhe priya-chikīrṣhavaḥ
source.translation: For I desire to observe those who are assembled here to fight, wishing to please in battle the evil-minded Duryodhana—the son of Dhritarashtra.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Krishna did as Arjuna asked, positioning the finest chariot between the two armies.
explanation: Responding to Arjuna's request, Krishna guides their splendid chariot to the exact spot between the two armies, right in front of the assembled kings and warriors, setting the stage for what Arjuna is about to see.

source.sanskrit:
संजय उवाच

एवमुक्तो हृषीकेशो गुडाकेशेन भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये स्थापयित्वा रथोत्तमम्।।1.24।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam ukto hṛiṣhīkeśho guḍākeśhena bhārata
senayor ubhayor madhye sthāpayitvā rathottamam
source.translation: Sanjaya said, Thus addressed by Arjuna, Krishna stationed the best of chariots, O Dhritarashtra, in the midst of the two armies.

simpleVersion: Standing before Bhishma, Drona, and all the assembled kings, Krishna tells Arjuna to look at the Kuru family gathered for war.
explanation: With the chariot now positioned between the armies, Krishna directs Arjuna's attention to the scene before him, right in front of Bhishma, Drona, and the other rulers, inviting him to truly see his extended family gathered for battle.

source.sanskrit:
भीष्मद्रोणप्रमुखतः सर्वेषां च महीक्षिताम्।

उवाच पार्थ पश्यैतान्समवेतान्कुरूनिति।।1.25।।
source.transliteration:
bhīṣhma-droṇa-pramukhataḥ sarveṣhāṁ cha mahī-kṣhitām
uvācha pārtha paśhyaitān samavetān kurūn iti
source.translation: In front of Bhishma and Drona, and all the rulers of the earth, he said: "O Arjuna, son of Pritha, behold these Kurus gathered together."

simpleVersion: Arjuna looks around and sees fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends standing in both armies.
explanation: As he looks across the battlefield, Arjuna begins to recognize the people standing before him, not enemies in the abstract, but his own relatives: fathers, grandfathers, teachers, uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and close friends.

source.sanskrit:
तत्रापश्यत्स्थितान्पार्थः पितृ़नथ पितामहान्।

आचार्यान्मातुलान्भ्रातृ़न्पुत्रान्पौत्रान्सखींस्तथा।।1.26।।
source.transliteration:
tatrāpaśhyat sthitān pārthaḥ pitṝīn atha pitāmahān
āchāryān mātulān bhrātṝīn putrān pautrān sakhīṁs tathā
source.translation: Then, Arjuna (son of Pritha) saw there (in the armies) stationed fathers, grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends.

simpleVersion: Arjuna also notices fathers-in-law and friends among the two armies, growing overwhelmed as he takes in the sight of his own family arrayed for war.
explanation: Continuing to scan the battlefield, Arjuna spots even more relatives, fathers-in-law and close friends, present in both armies. Seeing his kinsmen standing ready to fight begins to overwhelm him emotionally.

source.sanskrit:
श्वशुरान्सुहृदश्चैव सेनयोरुभयोरपि।

तान्समीक्ष्य स कौन्तेयः सर्वान्बन्धूनवस्थितान्।।1.27।।
source.transliteration: tān samīkṣhya sa kaunteyaḥ sarvān bandhūn avasthitān
source.translation: He saw fathers-in-law and friends in both the armies. The son of Kunti, Arjuna, seeing all those kinsmen thus standing arrayed.

simpleVersion: Overwhelmed with deep pity, Arjuna tells Krishna he cannot bear seeing his own people ready to fight each other.
explanation: Arjuna, overcome with sorrow, begins to speak. He tells Krishna that seeing his own kinsmen standing before him, eager for battle, has filled him with grief. (Note: the source translation for this verse is itself left incomplete mid-sentence, continuing directly into the next verse.)

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कृपया परयाऽऽविष्टो विषीदन्निदमब्रवीत्।

दृष्ट्वेमं स्वजनं कृष्ण युयुत्सुं समुपस्थितम्।।1.28।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kṛipayā parayāviṣhṭo viṣhīdann idam abravīt
dṛiṣhṭvemaṁ sva-janaṁ kṛiṣhṇa yuyutsuṁ samupasthitam
source.translation: Arjuna, overcome with deep pity, sorrowing, said: "O Krishna, seeing my kinsmen arrayed here, eager to fight,

simpleVersion: Arjuna describes his body reacting to shock and grief: his limbs weaken, his mouth goes dry, and he trembles all over.
explanation: Arjuna details the physical symptoms of his emotional collapse: his limbs feel weak, his mouth dries up, his body trembles, and his hair stands on end. This vivid description shows the depth of his inner turmoil.

source.sanskrit:
सीदन्ति मम गात्राणि मुखं च परिशुष्यति।

वेपथुश्च शरीरे मे रोमहर्षश्च जायते।।1.29।।
source.transliteration:
sīdanti mama gātrāṇi mukhaṁ cha pariśhuṣhyati
vepathuśh cha śharīre me roma-harṣhaśh cha jāyate
source.translation: My limbs fail, my mouth is parched, my body quivers, and my hair stands on end.

simpleVersion: His bow slips from his hand, his skin feels like it's burning, and his mind spins so much he can barely stand.
explanation: Arjuna's distress deepens. He can no longer hold his bow steady, his skin feels as if it's on fire, and he feels physically unable to stand upright as his mind spins out of control.

source.sanskrit:
गाण्डीवं स्रंसते हस्तात्त्वक्चैव परिदह्यते।

न च शक्नोम्यवस्थातुं भ्रमतीव च मे मनः।।1.30।।
source.transliteration:
gāṇḍīvaṁ sraṁsate hastāt tvak chaiva paridahyate
na cha śhaknomy avasthātuṁ bhramatīva cha me manaḥ
source.translation: The Gandiva slips from my hand, and my skin burns all over; I am unable to stand, and my mind is reeling, as it were.

simpleVersion: Arjuna sees bad omens all around and feels certain that nothing good can come from killing his own family in battle.
explanation: Arjuna interprets the atmosphere around him as filled with ill omens. He states plainly that he sees no benefit or good outcome that could justify killing his relatives in war.

source.sanskrit:
निमित्तानि च पश्यामि विपरीतानि केशव।

न च श्रेयोऽनुपश्यामि हत्वा स्वजनमाहवे।।1.31।।
source.transliteration:
nimittāni cha paśhyāmi viparītāni keśhava
na cha śhreyo ’nupaśhyāmi hatvā sva-janam āhave
source.translation: And I see ill omens, O Kesava. I do not see any good in slaying my kinsmen in battle.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he no longer wants victory, a kingdom, or comfort, and even questions the point of it all under these circumstances.
explanation: Arjuna declares he has lost all desire for the things he would normally fight for: victory, a kingdom, and personal happiness. He questions what value any of these could have if he must kill loved ones to get them.

source.sanskrit:
न काङ्क्षे विजयं कृष्ण न च राज्यं सुखानि च।

किं नो राज्येन गोविन्द किं भोगैर्जीवितेन वा।।1.32।।
source.transliteration:
na kāṅkṣhe vijayaṁ kṛiṣhṇa na cha rājyaṁ sukhāni cha
kiṁ no rājyena govinda kiṁ bhogair jīvitena vā
source.translation:
I desire not victory, O Krishna, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.
What use is dominion to us, O Krishna, or pleasures or even life?

simpleVersion: The very people he'd be fighting for, his elders and relatives, are the ones now standing in front of him, ready to risk everything.
explanation: Arjuna points out the irony of the situation: the kingdom and pleasures he might gain are meant to be enjoyed together with these same relatives. Yet those very people now stand ready to risk their lives in this war.

source.sanskrit:
येषामर्थे काङ्क्षितं नो राज्यं भोगाः सुखानि च।

त इमेऽवस्थिता युद्धे प्राणांस्त्यक्त्वा धनानि च।।1.33।।
source.transliteration:
yeṣhām arthe kāṅkṣhitaṁ no rājyaṁ bhogāḥ sukhāni cha
ta ime ’vasthitā yuddhe prāṇāṁs tyaktvā dhanāni cha
source.translation: Those for whose sake we desire kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures stand here in battle, having renounced life and wealth.

simpleVersion: Arjuna lists exactly who stands opposite him: teachers, fathers, sons, grandfathers, uncles, in-laws, grandsons, and other relatives.
explanation: Arjuna continues naming the categories of people arrayed against him, emphasizing just how many close relationships he would be severing through violence: teachers, father-figures, and several generations of family.

source.sanskrit:
आचार्याः पितरः पुत्रास्तथैव च पितामहाः।

मातुलाः श्चशुराः पौत्राः श्यालाः सम्बन्धिनस्तथा।।1.34।।
source.transliteration:
āchāryāḥ pitaraḥ putrās tathaiva cha pitāmahāḥ
mātulāḥ śhvaśhurāḥ pautrāḥ śhyālāḥ sambandhinas tathā
source.translation: Teachers, fathers, sons, and grandfathers, maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other relatives—

simpleVersion: Arjuna insists he won't kill these people even if it costs him his own life, let alone for the sake of ruling the whole world.
explanation: Arjuna firmly states his refusal. Even if these relatives were to kill him first, he still would not kill them, not even for the reward of ruling all three worlds, much less for something as small as earthly kingship.

source.sanskrit:
एतान्न हन्तुमिच्छामि घ्नतोऽपि मधुसूदन।

अपि त्रैलोक्यराज्यस्य हेतोः किं नु महीकृते।।1.35।।
source.transliteration:
etān na hantum ichchhāmi ghnato ’pi madhusūdana
api trailokya-rājyasya hetoḥ kiṁ nu mahī-kṛite
source.translation: These I do not wish to kill, O Krishna, even though they kill me, for the sake of dominion over the three worlds; leave alone killing them for the sake of the earth."

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks what joy could possibly come from killing Dhritarashtra's sons, believing it would only bring sin.
explanation: Arjuna questions the moral logic of the war. Even naming the opposing side as aggressors, he argues that killing them would bring no real happiness, only guilt and sin for those responsible.

source.sanskrit:
निहत्य धार्तराष्ट्रान्नः का प्रीतिः स्याज्जनार्दन।

पापमेवाश्रयेदस्मान्हत्वैतानाततायिनः।।1.36।।
source.transliteration:
nihatya dhārtarāṣhṭrān naḥ kā prītiḥ syāj janārdana
pāpam evāśhrayed asmān hatvaitān ātatāyinaḥ
source.translation: By killing these sons of Dhritarashtra, what pleasure could be ours, O Janardana? Only sin would accrue to us from killing these felons.

simpleVersion: Arjuna concludes that they should not kill their own relatives, since killing family could never bring true happiness.
explanation: Building on his previous point, Arjuna draws his conclusion: since killing brings only sin and no joy, they should not go through with killing Dhritarashtra's sons, who are their own relatives.

source.sanskrit:
तस्मान्नार्हा वयं हन्तुं धार्तराष्ट्रान्स्वबान्धवान्।

स्वजनं हि कथं हत्वा सुखिनः स्याम माधव।।1.37।।
source.transliteration:
tasmān nārhā vayaṁ hantuṁ dhārtarāṣhṭrān sa-bāndhavān 
sva-janaṁ hi kathaṁ hatvā sukhinaḥ syāma mādhava
source.translation: Therefore, we should not kill the sons of Dhritarashtra, our relatives; for how can we be happy by killing our own kin, O Madhava (Krishna)?

simpleVersion: Even though the enemy may be blinded by greed and can't see the wrongness of destroying families, Arjuna feels he must see it clearly.
explanation: Arjuna acknowledges that the enemy, driven by greed, cannot recognize the harm caused by destroying families or betraying friends. He implies that he and his side, however, should know better.

source.sanskrit:
यद्यप्येते न पश्यन्ति लोभोपहतचेतसः।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं मित्रद्रोहे च पातकम्।।1.38।।
source.transliteration:
yady apy ete na paśhyanti lobhopahata-chetasaḥ
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ mitra-drohe cha pātakam
source.translation: Though they, with intelligence overpowered by greed, see no evil in the destruction of families and no sin in hostility to friends,

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks why he and his side, who clearly see the harm in destroying a family, shouldn't choose to turn away from this sin.
explanation: Unlike the enemy, Arjuna argues that he and his side can clearly perceive the wrongness of destroying families through war. He asks why they wouldn't use that clarity to step back from committing this sin.

source.sanskrit:
कथं न ज्ञेयमस्माभिः पापादस्मान्निवर्तितुम्।

कुलक्षयकृतं दोषं प्रपश्यद्भिर्जनार्दन।।1.39।।
source.transliteration:
kathaṁ na jñeyam asmābhiḥ pāpād asmān nivartitum
kula-kṣhaya-kṛitaṁ doṣhaṁ prapaśhyadbhir janārdana
source.translation: Why should we not, who clearly see the evil in the destruction of families, learn to turn away from this sin, O Janardana (Krishna)?

simpleVersion: Arjuna explains that when a family is destroyed, its ancient traditions die out too, and disorder takes over where duty once stood.
explanation: Arjuna warns of the deeper consequences of war: destroying a family doesn't just end lives, it wipes out the sacred traditions passed down through generations. Once those traditions are lost, chaos overtakes the family entirely.

source.sanskrit:
कुलक्षये प्रणश्यन्ति कुलधर्माः सनातनाः।

धर्मे नष्टे कुलं कृत्स्नमधर्मोऽभिभवत्युत।।1.40।।
source.transliteration:
kula-kṣhaye praṇaśhyanti kula-dharmāḥ sanātanāḥ
dharme naṣhṭe kulaṁ kṛitsnam adharmo ’bhibhavaty uta
source.translation: In the destruction of a family, the immemorial religious rites of that family perish; on the destruction of spirituality, impiety indeed, overwhelms the whole family.

simpleVersion: Arjuna claims that when a family's moral order breaks down, its traditions and social structure begin to unravel as well.
explanation: Continuing his argument about the destruction of dharma, Arjuna states that when righteousness collapses in a family, it leads to a broader breakdown of the family's traditional social order, as this verse describes it.

source.sanskrit:
अधर्माभिभवात्कृष्ण प्रदुष्यन्ति कुलस्त्रियः।

स्त्रीषु दुष्टासु वार्ष्णेय जायते वर्णसङ्करः।।1.41।।
source.transliteration:
adharmābhibhavāt kṛiṣhṇa praduṣhyanti kula-striyaḥ
strīṣhu duṣhṭāsu vārṣhṇeya jāyate varṇa-saṅkaraḥ
source.translation: O Krishna, by the prevalence of impiety, the women of the family become corrupt; and, when women are corrupted, O Varshenya (descendant of Vrishni), intermingling of castes arises.

simpleVersion: Arjuna warns that this social breakdown condemns the family's ancestors, who lose the offerings that traditionally sustain them.
explanation: Arjuna continues describing the fallout: he believes this disorder harms both the living and the family's ancestors, who depend on ritual offerings of food and water that would no longer be properly performed.

source.sanskrit:
सङ्करो नरकायैव कुलघ्नानां कुलस्य च।

पतन्ति पितरो ह्येषां लुप्तपिण्डोदकक्रियाः।।1.42।।
source.transliteration:
saṅkaro narakāyaiva kula-ghnānāṁ kulasya cha
patanti pitaro hy eṣhāṁ lupta-piṇḍodaka-kriyāḥ
source.translation: Confusion of castes leads to hell for the slayers of the family, for their forebears fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and libations of water.

simpleVersion: Arjuna concludes that these wrongful acts destroy the family's long-standing sacred traditions completely.
explanation: Arjuna sums up this part of his argument: the destructive consequences he's described ultimately erase the eternal duties and rites that have defined and protected the family for generations.

source.sanskrit:
दोषैरेतैः कुलघ्नानां वर्णसङ्करकारकैः।

उत्साद्यन्ते जातिधर्माः कुलधर्माश्च शाश्वताः।।1.43।।
source.transliteration:
doṣhair etaiḥ kula-ghnānāṁ varṇa-saṅkara-kārakaiḥ
utsādyante jāti-dharmāḥ kula-dharmāśh cha śhāśhvatāḥ
source.translation: By these evil deeds of the destroyers of the family, which cause confusion of castes, the eternal religious rites of the caste and the family are destroyed.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he has heard that people from families whose sacred duties are destroyed are doomed to suffer in hell for a long time.
explanation: Arjuna cites a traditional belief he has heard: that people belonging to families where religious duties have collapsed are destined to endure punishment in hell for an indefinite period of time.

source.sanskrit:
उत्सन्नकुलधर्माणां मनुष्याणां जनार्दन।

नरकेऽनियतं वासो भवतीत्यनुशुश्रुम।।1.44।।
source.transliteration:
utsanna-kula-dharmāṇāṁ manuṣhyāṇāṁ janārdana
narake ‘niyataṁ vāso bhavatītyanuśhuśhruma
source.translation: We have heard, O Janardana, that those men in whose families the religious practices have been destroyed are inevitably destined to dwell in hell for an unknown period.

simpleVersion: Arjuna laments that he and his side are about to commit a terrible sin, driven by nothing more than greed for a kingdom's comforts.
explanation: Arjuna expresses deep regret, recognizing that the underlying motive for this war, greed for royal pleasures, is not worth the immense sin of killing one's own family.

source.sanskrit:
अहो बत महत्पापं कर्तुं व्यवसिता वयम्।

यद्राज्यसुखलोभेन हन्तुं स्वजनमुद्यताः।।1.45।।
source.transliteration:
aho bata mahat pāpaṁ kartuṁ vyavasitā vayam
yad rājya-sukha-lobhena hantuṁ sva-janam udyatāḥ
source.translation: Alas! We are involved in a great sin, for we are prepared to kill our kinsmen, out of greed for the pleasures of a kingdom.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he would rather be killed unarmed and without fighting back than go through with this war.
explanation: In deep despair, Arjuna declares he would prefer to die passively at the hands of Dhritarashtra's armed sons than to fight and kill his own relatives.

source.sanskrit:
यदि मामप्रतीकारमशस्त्रं शस्त्रपाणयः।

धार्तराष्ट्रा रणे हन्युस्तन्मे क्षेमतरं भवेत्।।1.46।।
source.transliteration:
yadi mām apratīkāram aśhastraṁ śhastra-pāṇayaḥ
dhārtarāṣhṭrā raṇe hanyus tan me kṣhemataraṁ bhavet
source.translation: If the sons of Dhritarashtra, with weapons in hand, should slay me in battle, unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya reports that Arjuna, overwhelmed with grief, drops his bow and arrows and sits down in his chariot.
explanation: Having finished expressing his anguish, Arjuna physically gives up: he throws down his bow and arrows and collapses onto the seat of his chariot, completely overcome by sorrow. This sets the stage for Krishna's teaching in Chapter 2.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वाऽर्जुनः संख्ये रथोपस्थ उपाविशत्।

विसृज्य सशरं चापं शोकसंविग्नमानसः।।1.47।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam uktvārjunaḥ saṅkhye rathopastha upāviśhat
visṛijya sa-śharaṁ chāpaṁ śhoka-saṁvigna-mānasaḥ
source.translation: Sanjaya said, Having thus spoken in the midst of the battlefield, Arjuna cast away his bow and arrow and, his mind overwhelmed with sorrow, sat down on the seat of the chariot.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Krishna spoke to Arjuna, who sat overwhelmed with pity, tears, and despair.
explanation: Sanjaya continues his report to the blind king. He describes Arjuna as consumed by pity, his eyes filled with tears, deeply agitated and despondent. It is at this moment that Krishna, called Madhusudana, begins to speak to him.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

तं तथा कृपयाऽविष्टमश्रुपूर्णाकुलेक्षणम्।

विषीदन्तमिदं वाक्यमुवाच मधुसूदनः।।2.1।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
taṁ tathā kṛipayāviṣhṭamaśhru pūrṇākulekṣhaṇam
viṣhīdantamidaṁ vākyam uvācha madhusūdanaḥ
source.translation: Sanjaya said: To him, who was thus overcome with pity, despondent, with eyes full of tears and agitated, Madhusudana (the destroyer of Madhu) or Krishna spoke these words.

simpleVersion: Krishna asks Arjuna where this un-Arjuna-like weakness has come from, calling it disgraceful and unworthy of him.
explanation: Krishna's first words are direct and challenging. He asks Arjuna where this sudden dejection has come from, telling him plainly that it is unbecoming of him, dishonorable, and will not lead him anywhere good.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

कुतस्त्वा कश्मलमिदं विषमे समुपस्थितम्।

अनार्यजुष्टमस्वर्ग्यमकीर्तिकरमर्जुन।।2.2।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
kutastvā kaśhmalamidaṁ viṣhame samupasthitam
anārya-juṣhṭamaswargyam akīrti-karam arjuna
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "From whence has this perilous strait come upon you, this dejection which is unworthy of you, disgraceful, and which will close the gates of heaven upon you, O Arjuna?"

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna not to give in to weakness, since it doesn't suit him, and to stand up and fight.
explanation: Krishna pushes back firmly against Arjuna's collapse. He tells him this small-mindedness does not belong to someone of his caliber, and urges him to cast it off and rise to face the battle ahead.
lifeLesson: Sometimes the most caring response to someone's despair is a firm push to get back up, not just sympathy.

source.sanskrit:
क्लैब्यं मा स्म गमः पार्थ नैतत्त्वय्युपपद्यते।

क्षुद्रं हृदयदौर्बल्यं त्यक्त्वोत्तिष्ठ परन्तप।।2.3।।
source.transliteration:
klaibyaṁ mā sma gamaḥ pārtha naitat tvayyupapadyate
kṣhudraṁ hṛidaya-daurbalyaṁ tyaktvottiṣhṭha parantapa
source.translation: Do not yield to impotence, O Arjuna, son of Pritha. It does not befit you. Cast off this mean weakness of the heart! Stand up, O conqueror of foes!

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks how he could possibly shoot arrows at Bhishma and Drona, men he deeply respects and reveres.
explanation: Arjuna pushes back against Krishna's challenge. He asks how he could possibly take up arms against Bhishma and Drona, two men he considers worthy of worship, not violence.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

कथं भीष्ममहं संख्ये द्रोणं च मधुसूदन।

इषुभिः प्रतियोत्स्यामि पूजार्हावरिसूदन।।2.4।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
kathaṁ bhīṣhmam ahaṁ sankhye droṇaṁ cha madhusūdana
iṣhubhiḥ pratiyotsyāmi pūjārhāvari-sūdana
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Madhusudana, how can I fight in battle with arrows against Bhishma and Drona, who are worthy of being worshipped, O destroyer of enemies?"

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he'd rather live on alms than kill his noble teachers, since victory gained that way would be stained with their blood.
explanation: Arjuna explains his reasoning further. He would rather beg for his food than kill such respected teachers, because any wealth or pleasure won by their deaths would forever feel stained with their blood.

source.sanskrit:
गुरूनहत्वा हि महानुभावान्

श्रेयो भोक्तुं भैक्ष्यमपीह लोके।

हत्वार्थकामांस्तु गुरूनिहैव

भुञ्जीय भोगान् रुधिरप्रदिग्धान्।।2.5।।
source.transliteration:
gurūnahatvā hi mahānubhāvān
śhreyo bhoktuṁ bhaikṣhyamapīha loke
hatvārtha-kāmāṁstu gurūnihaiva
bhuñjīya bhogān rudhira-pradigdhān
source.translation: Better it is, indeed, in this world to accept alms than to slay the most noble teachers. But if I were to kill them, even in this world, all my enjoyments of wealth and fulfilled desires would be stained with their blood.

simpleVersion: Arjuna admits he can't tell whether winning or losing would be worse, since the people he'd have to kill stand right before him.
explanation: Arjuna confesses deep uncertainty. He genuinely doesn't know which outcome would be better, conquering or being conquered, since the very people he doesn't wish to kill are standing directly in front of him, ready for war.

source.sanskrit:
न चैतद्विद्मः कतरन्नो गरीयो

यद्वा जयेम यदि वा नो जयेयुः।

यानेव हत्वा न जिजीविषाम

स्तेऽवस्थिताः प्रमुखे धार्तराष्ट्राः।।2.6।।
source.transliteration:
na chaitadvidmaḥ kataranno garīyo
yadvā jayema yadi vā no jayeyuḥ
yāneva hatvā na jijīviṣhāmas
te ’vasthitāḥ pramukhe dhārtarāṣhṭrāḥ
source.translation: I can hardly tell which would be better, that we should conquer them or that they should conquer us. Even the sons of Dhritarashtra, whom we do not wish to slay, stand facing us.

simpleVersion: Confused about his duty, Arjuna asks Krishna to tell him clearly what is right, declaring himself Krishna's student.
explanation: Arjuna's resistance turns into surrender. Overwhelmed and unsure of his duty, he openly asks Krishna to tell him decisively what path is right, and declares himself Krishna's disciple, ready to be taught.

source.sanskrit:
कार्पण्यदोषोपहतस्वभावः

पृच्छामि त्वां धर्मसंमूढचेताः।

यच्छ्रेयः स्यान्निश्िचतं ब्रूहि तन्मे

शिष्यस्तेऽहं शाधि मां त्वां प्रपन्नम्।।2.7।।
source.transliteration:
kārpaṇya-doṣhopahata-svabhāvaḥ
pṛichchhāmi tvāṁ dharma-sammūḍha-chetāḥ
yach-chhreyaḥ syānniśhchitaṁ brūhi tanme
śhiṣhyaste ’haṁ śhādhi māṁ tvāṁ prapannam
source.translation: My heart is overpowered by the taint of pity; my mind is confused as to my duty. I ask Thee: Tell me decisively what is good for me. I am Thy disciple; instruct me, who has taken refuge in Thee.

simpleVersion: Arjuna says he can't imagine anything, even ruling the whole earth or the heavens, that would remove this grief burning inside him.
explanation: Arjuna expresses the depth of his despair. He says that even gaining unrivaled power on earth, or lordship over the gods themselves, would not be enough to burn away the sorrow consuming him right now.

source.sanskrit:
न हि प्रपश्यामि ममापनुद्या

द्यच्छोकमुच्छोषणमिन्द्रियाणाम्।

अवाप्य भूमावसपत्नमृद्धम्

राज्यं सुराणामपि चाधिपत्यम्।।2.8।।
source.transliteration:
na hi prapaśhyāmi mamāpanudyād
yach-chhokam uchchhoṣhaṇam-indriyāṇām
avāpya bhūmāv-asapatnamṛiddhaṁ
rājyaṁ surāṇāmapi chādhipatyam
source.translation: I do not see that this sorrow that burns up my senses would be removed, even if I were to attain prosperous and unrivaled dominion on earth or lordship over the gods.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya reports that after saying this to Krishna, Arjuna declared 'I will not fight' and fell completely silent.
explanation: Having said all this to Krishna, Arjuna reaches his final point: he flatly states he will not fight, then falls silent. This marks the end of Arjuna's despair and sets the stage for Krishna's teaching.

source.sanskrit:
सञ्जय उवाच

एवमुक्त्वा हृषीकेशं गुडाकेशः परन्तप।

न योत्स्य इति गोविन्दमुक्त्वा तूष्णीं बभूव ह।।2.9।।
source.transliteration:
sañjaya uvācha
evam-uktvā hṛiṣhīkeśhaṁ guḍākeśhaḥ parantapa
na yotsya iti govindam uktvā tūṣhṇīṁ babhūva ha
source.translation: Sanjaya said: Having spoken thus to Hrishikesha, the Lord of the senses, Arjuna, the conqueror of sleep and destroyer of foes, said, "I will not fight," and became silent.

simpleVersion: Sanjaya tells Dhritarashtra that Krishna, smiling, then spoke to the despondent Arjuna standing between the two armies.
explanation: Sanjaya notes a striking detail: even as Arjuna sits in despair between the two armies, Krishna responds with a smile before He begins to speak, signaling the wisdom about to be shared.

source.sanskrit:
तमुवाच हृषीकेशः प्रहसन्निव भारत।

सेनयोरुभयोर्मध्ये विषीदन्तमिदं वचः।।2.10।।
source.transliteration:
tam-uvācha hṛiṣhīkeśhaḥ prahasanniva bhārata
senayorubhayor-madhye viṣhīdantam-idaṁ vachaḥ
source.translation: To him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies, Krishna, smiling, O Bharata, spoke these words.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna he grieves for those who don't need grieving, even while sounding wise, since the truly wise grieve for no one.
explanation: Krishna begins His teaching with a gentle but pointed correction. He tells Arjuna that his grief, though dressed up in wise-sounding words, is misplaced, because those who truly understand life do not grieve for the living or the dead.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

अशोच्यानन्वशोचस्त्वं प्रज्ञावादांश्च भाषसे।

गतासूनगतासूंश्च नानुशोचन्ति पण्डिताः।।2.11।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
aśhochyān-anvaśhochas-tvaṁ prajñā-vādānśh cha bhāṣhase
gatāsūn-agatāsūnśh-cha nānuśhochanti paṇḍitāḥ
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for; yet, you speak words of wisdom. The wise grieve neither for the living nor for the dead."

simpleVersion: Krishna says there was never a time He, Arjuna, or these kings did not exist, nor will they ever cease to exist.
explanation: Krishna introduces one of the Gita's central ideas: existence itself is continuous. He, Arjuna, and everyone present have always existed in some form, and will continue to exist in the future as well.

source.sanskrit:
न त्वेवाहं जातु नासं न त्वं नेमे जनाधिपाः।

न चैव न भविष्यामः सर्वे वयमतः परम्।।2.12।।
source.transliteration:
na tvevāhaṁ jātu nāsaṁ na tvaṁ neme janādhipāḥ
na chaiva na bhaviṣhyāmaḥ sarve vayamataḥ param
source.translation: Nor, at any time, was I not, nor thou, nor these rulers of men; nor, verily, shall we ever cease to be hereafter.

simpleVersion: Just as a person moves through childhood, youth, and old age, the soul moves into another body; the wise don't grieve.
explanation: Krishna offers a simple, relatable image: just as the body changes from childhood to old age without the self being lost, the soul similarly moves on to a new body at death. Someone who understands this doesn't grieve over it.
lifeLesson: Change of form, whether in age or in death, doesn't have to mean loss of self.

source.sanskrit:
देहिनोऽस्मिन्यथा देहे कौमारं यौवनं जरा।

तथा देहान्तरप्राप्तिर्धीरस्तत्र न मुह्यति।।2.13।।
source.transliteration:
dehino ’smin yathā dehe kaumāraṁ yauvanaṁ jarā
tathā dehāntara-prāptir dhīras tatra na muhyati
source.translation: Just as the embodied soul passes through childhood, youth, and old age in this body, so too does it pass into another body; the steadfast one does not grieve over this.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that sensations like heat, cold, pleasure, and pain come and go, so he should learn to endure them patiently.
explanation: Krishna points out that the sensory experiences of comfort and discomfort are temporary by nature; they arise and pass away. He instructs Arjuna to bear them steadily rather than be shaken by them.
lifeLesson: Discomfort and pleasure both pass. Learning to sit with either without being ruled by it builds real steadiness.

source.sanskrit:
मात्रास्पर्शास्तु कौन्तेय शीतोष्णसुखदुःखदाः।

आगमापायिनोऽनित्यास्तांस्तितिक्षस्व भारत।।2.14।।
source.transliteration:
mātrā-sparśhās tu kaunteya śhītoṣhṇa-sukha-duḥkha-dāḥ
āgamāpāyino ’nityās tans-titikṣhasva bhārata
source.translation: The contact of the senses with the objects, O son of Kunti, which causes heat and cold, pleasure and pain, has a beginning and an end; they are impermanent; endure them bravely, O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the person unaffected by pleasure and pain, treating both the same, becomes fit for true, lasting freedom.
explanation: Krishna describes a specific quality of inner strength: someone who remains steady regardless of pleasure or pain becomes capable of reaching a state of lasting peace, described here as immortality.

source.sanskrit:
यं हि न व्यथयन्त्येते पुरुषं पुरुषर्षभ।

समदुःखसुखं धीरं सोऽमृतत्वाय कल्पते।।2.15।।
source.transliteration:
yaṁ hi na vyathayantyete puruṣhaṁ puruṣharṣhabha
sama-duḥkha-sukhaṁ dhīraṁ so ’mṛitatvāya kalpate
source.translation: That firm man, whom surely these afflictions do not, O chief among men, to whom pleasure and pain are the same, is fit for attaining immortality.

simpleVersion: Krishna explains that what is unreal never truly exists, and what is real never stops existing; those with true insight understand this difference.
explanation: Krishna draws a clear line between the permanent and the temporary. He says that anything unreal or fleeting has no lasting existence, while what is truly real can never cease to be, a truth seen only by those with deep insight.

source.sanskrit:
नासतो विद्यते भावो नाभावो विद्यते सतः।

उभयोरपि दृष्टोऽन्तस्त्वनयोस्तत्त्वदर्शिभिः।।2.16।।
source.transliteration:
nāsato vidyate bhāvo nābhāvo vidyate sataḥ
ubhayorapi dṛiṣhṭo ’nta stvanayos tattva-darśhibhiḥ
source.translation: The unreal has no being; there is no non-being of the real; the truth about both has been seen by the knowers of the truth (or the seers of the essence).

simpleVersion: Krishna says to understand that whatever pervades everything is indestructible, and nothing can destroy that imperishable reality.
explanation: Krishna points Arjuna toward the one thing in existence that cannot be destroyed: the essence that pervades everything. Unlike bodies or objects, this underlying reality cannot be ended by anyone or anything.

source.sanskrit:
अविनाशि तु तद्विद्धि येन सर्वमिदं ततम्।

विनाशमव्ययस्यास्य न कश्चित् कर्तुमर्हति।।2.17।।
source.transliteration:
avināśhi tu tadviddhi yena sarvam idaṁ tatam
vināśham avyayasyāsya na kaśhchit kartum arhati
source.translation: Know that to be indestructible, by which all this is pervaded. No one can cause the destruction of that, the Imperishable.

simpleVersion: Krishna explains that only the body of the eternal soul comes to an end, so he tells Arjuna to go ahead and fight.
explanation: Krishna clarifies the distinction between body and soul. The bodies people wear are temporary and will end, but the soul within them is eternal and beyond measure. Because of this, He directly tells Arjuna to fight.

source.sanskrit:
अन्तवन्त इमे देहा नित्यस्योक्ताः शरीरिणः।

अनाशिनोऽप्रमेयस्य तस्माद्युध्यस्व भारत।।2.18।।
source.transliteration:
antavanta ime dehā nityasyoktāḥ śharīriṇaḥ
anāśhino ’prameyasya tasmād yudhyasva bhārata
source.translation: These bodies of the embodied Self, which are eternal, indestructible, and immeasurable, are said to have an end. Therefore, fight, O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: Krishna says both the one who thinks the soul kills, and the one who thinks it is killed, are mistaken.
explanation: Krishna challenges a common misunderstanding. He says that anyone who believes the soul can kill, or that it can be killed, doesn't actually understand its true nature, because the soul is beyond the act of killing altogether.

source.sanskrit:
य एनं वेत्ति हन्तारं यश्चैनं मन्यते हतम्।

उभौ तौ न विजानीतो नायं हन्ति न हन्यते।।2.19।।
source.transliteration:
ya enaṁ vetti hantāraṁ yaśh chainaṁ manyate hatam
ubhau tau na vijānīto nāyaṁ hanti na hanyate
source.translation: He who takes the Self to be the slayer and he who thinks it is slain, neither of them knows. It does not slay, nor is it slain.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the soul is never born and never dies; it is unborn, eternal, and unchanging, and remains untouched even when the body dies.
explanation: Krishna describes the soul in absolute terms: it has no birth and no death, it does not come into being or cease to exist, and it remains constant and ancient. Even when a body is destroyed, the soul within it is unaffected.

source.sanskrit:
न जायते म्रियते वा कदाचि

न्नायं भूत्वा भविता वा न भूयः।

अजो नित्यः शाश्वतोऽयं पुराणो

न हन्यते हन्यमाने शरीरे।।2.20।।
source.transliteration:
na jāyate mriyate vā kadāchin
nāyaṁ bhūtvā bhavitā vā na bhūyaḥ
ajo nityaḥ śhāśhvato ’yaṁ purāṇo
na hanyate hanyamāne śharīre
source.translation: It is not born, nor does it ever die; after having been, it again does not cease to be; unborn, eternal, changeless, and ancient, it is not killed when the body is killed.

simpleVersion: Krishna asks Arjuna how someone who truly knows the soul is indestructible and eternal could possibly cause anyone to be killed.
explanation: Krishna poses a pointed question: if a person genuinely understands that the soul is unborn and imperishable, how could that same person believe they are capable of killing or causing death at all?

source.sanskrit:
वेदाविनाशिनं नित्यं य एनमजमव्ययम्।

कथं स पुरुषः पार्थ कं घातयति हन्ति कम्।।2.21।।
source.transliteration:
vedāvināśhinaṁ nityaṁ ya enam ajam avyayam
kathaṁ sa puruṣhaḥ pārtha kaṁ ghātayati hanti kam
source.translation: Whoever knows it to be indestructible, eternal, unborn, and inexhaustible, how can that person slay, O Arjuna, or cause to be slain?

simpleVersion: Just as a person discards worn-out clothes for new ones, the soul leaves behind an old body and takes on a new one.
explanation: Krishna offers one of the Gita's most famous images: death is like changing clothes. Just as a person swaps out worn garments for new ones, the soul simply moves from an old, worn-out body into a new one.

source.sanskrit:
वासांसि जीर्णानि यथा विहाय

नवानि गृह्णाति नरोऽपराणि।

तथा शरीराणि विहाय जीर्णा

न्यन्यानि संयाति नवानि देही।।2.22।।
source.transliteration:
vāsānsi jīrṇāni yathā vihāya
navāni gṛihṇāti naro ’parāṇi
tathā śharīrāṇi vihāya jīrṇānya
nyāni sanyāti navāni dehī
source.translation: Just as a man casts off worn-out clothes and puts on new ones, so too the embodied Self casts off worn-out bodies and enters others that are new.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the soul cannot be cut by weapons, burned by fire, soaked by water, or dried out by wind.
explanation: Krishna continues describing the soul's indestructible nature using concrete physical examples. No weapon, no fire, no water, and no wind, the forces that destroy ordinary things, can affect it in any way.

source.sanskrit:
नैनं छिन्दन्ति शस्त्राणि नैनं दहति पावकः।

न चैनं क्लेदयन्त्यापो न शोषयति मारुतः।।2.23।।
source.transliteration:
nainaṁ chhindanti śhastrāṇi nainaṁ dahati pāvakaḥ
na chainaṁ kledayantyāpo na śhoṣhayati mārutaḥ
source.translation: Weapons cannot cut it, fire cannot burn it, water cannot wet it, wind cannot dry it.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the soul cannot be cut, burned, soaked, or dried; it is eternal, everywhere, unmoving, and unchanging.
explanation: Krishna reinforces the previous verse, listing the soul's qualities directly: it resists all forms of physical destruction, exists everywhere, remains stable and unmoving, and has always existed.

source.sanskrit:
अच्छेद्योऽयमदाह्योऽयमक्लेद्योऽशोष्य एव च।

नित्यः सर्वगतः स्थाणुरचलोऽयं सनातनः।।2.24।।
source.transliteration:
achchhedyo ’yam adāhyo ’yam akledyo ’śhoṣhya eva cha
nityaḥ sarva-gataḥ sthāṇur achalo ’yaṁ sanātanaḥ
source.translation: This Self cannot be cut, burned, wetted, nor dried up; it is eternal, all-pervasive, stable, immovable, and ancient.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the soul is unseen, beyond thought, and unchanging, so knowing this, Arjuna has no real reason to grieve.
explanation: Krishna concludes this section of teaching by describing the soul as something beyond ordinary perception and thought, and completely unchanging. Given this understanding, He tells Arjuna he has no valid reason left to grieve.

source.sanskrit:
अव्यक्तोऽयमचिन्त्योऽयमविकार्योऽयमुच्यते।

तस्मादेवं विदित्वैनं नानुशोचितुमर्हसि।।2.25।।
source.transliteration:
avyakto ’yam achintyo ’yam avikāryo ’yam uchyate
tasmādevaṁ viditvainaṁ nānuśhochitum arhasi
source.translation: This Self is said to be unmanifested, unthinkable, and unchangeable. Therefore, knowing this to be so, you should not grieve.

simpleVersion: Even if Arjuna believed the soul is constantly born and constantly dying, Krishna says he still shouldn't grieve.
explanation: Krishna offers a second angle, in case Arjuna isn't convinced by the previous argument. Even under the alternate belief that the soul is repeatedly born and dies again and again, grief would still not be the right response.

source.sanskrit:
अथ चैनं नित्यजातं नित्यं वा मन्यसे मृतम्।

तथापि त्वं महाबाहो नैवं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.26।।
source.transliteration:
atha chainaṁ nitya-jātaṁ nityaṁ vā manyase mṛitam
tathāpi tvaṁ mahā-bāho naivaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: But even if thou thinkest of It as constantly being born and constantly dying, even then, O mighty-armed one, thou shouldst not grieve.

simpleVersion: Krishna reminds Arjuna that death is certain for the born, and birth is certain for the dead, so don't grieve over the unavoidable.
explanation: Krishna states a basic, unavoidable fact of existence: whoever is born will die, and whoever dies will be born again. Since this cycle cannot be changed, he tells Arjuna there's no sense in grieving over it.
lifeLesson: Grieving over what is truly unavoidable rarely changes the outcome; it only adds suffering to what already has to be faced.

source.sanskrit:
जातस्य हि ध्रुवो मृत्युर्ध्रुवं जन्म मृतस्य च।

तस्मादपरिहार्येऽर्थे न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.27।।
source.transliteration:
jātasya hi dhruvo mṛityur dhruvaṁ janma mṛitasya cha
tasmād aparihārye ’rthe na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: For the born, death is certain, and for the dead, birth is certain; therefore, you should not grieve over the inevitable.

simpleVersion: Krishna says beings are unseen before birth, visible in the middle of life, and unseen again after death, so what is there to grieve?
explanation: Krishna describes life as a kind of bracket surrounded by mystery: unseen before it starts, briefly visible while it lasts, and unseen again once it ends. Given this pattern, he questions what there really is to mourn.

source.sanskrit:
अव्यक्तादीनि भूतानि व्यक्तमध्यानि भारत।

अव्यक्तनिधनान्येव तत्र का परिदेवना।।2.28।।
source.transliteration:
avyaktādīni bhūtāni vyakta-madhyāni bhārata
avyakta-nidhanānyeva tatra kā paridevanā
source.translation: Beings are unmanifest in their beginning, manifest in their middle state, O Arjuna, and unmanifest again in their end. What is there to grieve about?

simpleVersion: Krishna says some see the soul with wonder, some speak of it with wonder, yet even after hearing, hardly anyone understands it.
explanation: Krishna acknowledges how mysterious and difficult this subject truly is. People may view it, describe it, or hear about it with a sense of awe, yet genuine understanding of the soul remains rare, even after all that.

source.sanskrit:
आश्चर्यवत्पश्यति कश्चिदेन

माश्चर्यवद्वदति तथैव चान्यः।

आश्चर्यवच्चैनमन्यः श्रृणोति

श्रुत्वाप्येनं वेद न चैव कश्चित्।।2.29।।
source.transliteration:
āśhcharya-vat paśhyati kaśhchid enan
āśhcharya-vad vadati tathaiva chānyaḥ
āśhcharya-vach chainam anyaḥ śhṛiṇoti
śhrutvāpyenaṁ veda na chaiva kaśhchit
source.translation: One sees this (the Self) as a wonder; another speaks of it as a wonder; another hears of it as a wonder; yet, having heard, none understands it at all.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the soul within every being is always indestructible, so Arjuna should not grieve for any living creature.
explanation: Krishna brings this section of teaching to a close with a direct instruction. Because the true self within every being is permanently beyond destruction, He tells Arjuna he has no reason to grieve for any creature at all.

source.sanskrit:
देही नित्यमवध्योऽयं देहे सर्वस्य भारत।

तस्मात्सर्वाणि भूतानि न त्वं शोचितुमर्हसि।।2.30।।
source.transliteration:
dehī nityam avadhyo ’yaṁ dehe sarvasya bhārata
tasmāt sarvāṇi bhūtāni na tvaṁ śhochitum arhasi
source.translation: This indweller in the body of everyone is ever indestructible, O Arjuna; therefore, you should not grieve for any creature.

simpleVersion: Krishna shifts to a new argument, reminding Arjuna of his duty as a warrior, saying nothing is better for a Kshatriya than a righteous battle.
explanation: Krishna changes approach, moving from the nature of the soul to Arjuna's specific role in life. As a warrior, he says, there is nothing more fitting or valuable for Arjuna than fighting in a just war.

source.sanskrit:
स्वधर्ममपि चावेक्ष्य न विकम्पितुमर्हसि।

धर्म्याद्धि युद्धाछ्रेयोऽन्यत्क्षत्रियस्य न विद्यते।।2.31।।
source.transliteration:
swa-dharmam api chāvekṣhya na vikampitum arhasi
dharmyāddhi yuddhāch chhreyo ’nyat kṣhatriyasya na vidyate
source.translation: Further, having regard to your duty, you should not waver, for there is nothing higher for a Kshatriya than a righteous war.

simpleVersion: Krishna says fortunate are the warriors who get the chance to fight in a battle like an open door to heaven.
explanation: Krishna frames the coming battle in a positive light for a warrior like Arjuna. This kind of righteous, unsought war, he says, is a rare opportunity that most warriors would consider fortunate to be given.

source.sanskrit:
यदृच्छया चोपपन्नं स्वर्गद्वारमपावृतम्।

सुखिनः क्षत्रियाः पार्थ लभन्ते युद्धमीदृशम्।।2.32।।
source.transliteration:
yadṛichchhayā chopapannaṁ swarga-dvāram apāvṛitam
sukhinaḥ kṣhatriyāḥ pārtha labhante yuddham īdṛiśham
source.translation: Happy are the Kshatriyas, O Arjuna! who are called to fight in such a battle that comes of its own accord as an open door to heaven.

simpleVersion: Krishna warns Arjuna that refusing to fight this righteous war means abandoning his duty and reputation, and bringing sin upon himself.
explanation: Krishna presents a warning as motivation. If Arjuna chooses not to fight this rightful war, he says Arjuna will fail in his duty, damage his good name, and take on sin as a result.

source.sanskrit:
अथ चैत्त्वमिमं धर्म्यं संग्रामं न करिष्यसि।

ततः स्वधर्मं कीर्तिं च हित्वा पापमवाप्स्यसि।।2.33।।
source.transliteration:
atha chet tvam imaṁ dharmyaṁ saṅgrāmaṁ na kariṣhyasi
tataḥ sva-dharmaṁ kīrtiṁ cha hitvā pāpam avāpsyasi
source.translation: But if you will not fight this righteous war, then having abandoned your own duty and reputation, you will incur sin.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that people will forever speak of his dishonor, and for someone once honored, dishonor is worse than death itself.
explanation: Krishna continues His warning, pointing to the social consequences of backing out. He says people will always remember and repeat the story of Arjuna's disgrace, and for a man of Arjuna's stature, that kind of shame would hurt more than dying.

source.sanskrit:
अकीर्तिं चापि भूतानि कथयिष्यन्ति तेऽव्ययाम्।

संभावितस्य चाकीर्तिर्मरणादतिरिच्यते।।2.34।।
source.transliteration:
akīrtiṁ chāpi bhūtāni
kathayiṣhyanti te ’vyayām
sambhāvitasya chākīrtir
maraṇād atirichyate
source.translation: People will also recount your everlasting dishonor; and for one who has been honored, dishonor is worse than death.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the great warriors will assume Arjuna withdrew out of fear, and those who respected him will start thinking less of him.
explanation: Krishna spells out how Arjuna's withdrawal would actually be perceived. Fellow warriors, rather than seeing restraint or compassion, would assume cowardice, and the respect Arjuna has earned would quickly turn into contempt.

source.sanskrit:
भयाद्रणादुपरतं मंस्यन्ते त्वां महारथाः।

येषां च त्वं बहुमतो भूत्वा यास्यसि लाघवम्।।2.35।।
source.transliteration:
bhayād raṇād uparataṁ mansyante tvāṁ mahā-rathāḥ
yeṣhāṁ cha tvaṁ bahu-mato bhūtvā yāsyasi lāghavam
source.translation: The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear, and you will be held in low esteem by those who have held you in high regard.

simpleVersion: Krishna says Arjuna's enemies will mock his abilities and speak many hurtful words, and nothing could be more painful than that.
explanation: Krishna adds one more consequence: his enemies would take the opportunity to insult and belittle him publicly. He suggests that this kind of humiliation would be even harder to bear than the pain of battle itself.

source.sanskrit:
अवाच्यवादांश्च बहून् वदिष्यन्ति तवाहिताः।

निन्दन्तस्तव सामर्थ्यं ततो दुःखतरं नु किम्।।2.36।।
source.transliteration:
avāchya-vādānśh cha bahūn vadiṣhyanti tavāhitāḥ
nindantastava sāmarthyaṁ tato duḥkhataraṁ nu kim
source.translation: Your enemies, scoffing at your power, will speak many abusive words—what could be more painful than this?

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that dying he gains heaven, winning he enjoys the earth, so he should rise and fight with resolve.
explanation: Krishna reframes the choice in front of Arjuna as one with no truly bad outcome. Whether he dies in battle or survives victorious, something good awaits him either way, so Krishna urges him to stand and commit to fighting.

source.sanskrit:
हतो वा प्राप्स्यसि स्वर्गं जित्वा वा भोक्ष्यसे महीम्।

तस्मादुत्तिष्ठ कौन्तेय युद्धाय कृतनिश्चयः।।2.37।।
source.transliteration:
hato vā prāpsyasi swargaṁ jitvā vā bhokṣhyase mahīm
tasmād uttiṣhṭha kaunteya yuddhāya kṛita-niśhchayaḥ
source.translation: Slain, you will obtain heaven; victorious, you will enjoy the earth; therefore, stand up, O son of Kunti, resolved to fight.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to treat pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat as equal, and fight simply because it's his duty.
explanation: Krishna introduces a key principle: approaching action with equanimity. If Arjuna fights while treating outcomes like pleasure, pain, gain, or loss as equal, and acts purely out of duty, he will not incur sin from the act itself.
lifeLesson: Acting from duty rather than from attachment to the outcome is what keeps action from becoming a burden.

source.sanskrit:
सुखदुःखे समे कृत्वा लाभालाभौ जयाजयौ।

ततो युद्धाय युज्यस्व नैवं पापमवाप्स्यसि।।2.38।।
source.transliteration:
sukha-duḥkhe same kṛitvā lābhālābhau jayājayau
tato yuddhāya yujyasva naivaṁ pāpam avāpsyasi
source.translation: Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat equal, engage in battle for the sake of battle; thus, you shall not incur sin.

simpleVersion: Krishna says He has now explained the wisdom of knowledge, and tells Arjuna to listen next to the wisdom of Yoga.
explanation: Krishna marks a turning point in His teaching. Having explained the philosophical understanding of the soul, He now shifts to teaching the practical path of Yoga, action performed skillfully, which will free Arjuna from being bound by his actions.

source.sanskrit:
एषा तेऽभिहिता सांख्ये बुद्धिर्योगे त्विमां श्रृणु।

बुद्ध्यायुक्तो यया पार्थ कर्मबन्धं प्रहास्यसि।।2.39।।
source.transliteration:
eṣhā te ’bhihitā sānkhye
buddhir yoge tvimāṁ śhṛiṇu
buddhyā yukto yayā pārtha
karma-bandhaṁ prahāsyasi
source.translation: This, which has been taught to you, is wisdom concerning Sankhya. Now listen to wisdom concerning Yoga, endowed with which, O Arjuna, you shall cast off the bonds of action.

simpleVersion: Krishna says on this path no effort is wasted; even a small amount of this practice protects one from great fear.
explanation: Krishna offers reassurance about starting this path. Unlike many undertakings where effort can be wasted or backfire, even a small step on this path brings real benefit and offers protection from deep fear.
lifeLesson: Even a small, sincere effort on the right path is never wasted, however far off the goal may seem.

source.sanskrit:
नेहाभिक्रमनाशोऽस्ति प्रत्यवायो न विद्यते।

स्वल्पमप्यस्य धर्मस्य त्रायते महतो भयात्।।2.40।।
source.transliteration:
nehābhikrama-nāśho ’sti pratyavāyo na vidyate
svalpam apyasya dharmasya trāyate mahato bhayāt
source.translation: In this, there is no loss of effort, nor is there any harm produced, nor any transgression. Even a little of this knowledge protects one from great fear.

simpleVersion: Krishna says on this path there is one clear, resolved intention, but the minds of the undecided branch out endlessly in many directions.
explanation: Krishna contrasts focused determination with indecision. A person walking this path holds a single, clear intention, while someone who hasn't committed ends up with countless scattered, conflicting thoughts pulling them in different directions.

source.sanskrit:
व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिरेकेह कुरुनन्दन।

बहुशाखा ह्यनन्ताश्च बुद्धयोऽव्यवसायिनाम्।।2.41।।
source.transliteration:
vyavasāyātmikā buddhir ekeha kuru-nandana
bahu-śhākhā hyanantāśh cha buddhayo ’vyavasāyinām
source.translation: Here, O joy of the Kurus, there is only one single-pointed determination; many-branched and endless are the thoughts of the indecisive.

simpleVersion: Krishna describes people who lack real wisdom, delighting in flowery scriptural language and insisting that nothing beyond it exists.
explanation: Krishna begins a gentle critique. He describes a certain kind of person who takes pleasure in elaborate, ornamental religious language, believing that reciting or following such words is the whole of spiritual life, with nothing more to it.

source.sanskrit:
यामिमां पुष्पितां वाचं प्रवदन्त्यविपश्चितः।

वेदवादरताः पार्थ नान्यदस्तीति वादिनः।।2.42।।
source.transliteration:
yāmimāṁ puṣhpitāṁ vāchaṁ pravadanty-avipaśhchitaḥ
veda-vāda-ratāḥ pārtha nānyad astīti vādinaḥ
source.translation: The unwise, taking pleasure in the eulogizing words of the Vedas, utter flowery speech, saying, "There is nothing else," O Arjuna.

simpleVersion: Krishna says these people are driven by desire, chase heaven as their goal, and perform many elaborate rituals aimed at pleasure and power.
explanation: Krishna continues describing this mindset. Such people are motivated mainly by personal desire, aiming for heavenly rewards and worldly pleasure and power, and they pursue this through many detailed, ritualistic actions rather than deeper understanding.

source.sanskrit:
कामात्मानः स्वर्गपरा जन्मकर्मफलप्रदाम्।

क्रियाविशेषबहुलां भोगैश्वर्यगतिं प्रति।।2.43।।
source.transliteration:
kāmātmānaḥ svarga-parā 

 janma-karma-phala-pradām

 kriyā-viśeṣa-bahulāṁ

 bhogaiśvarya-gatiṁ prati
source.translation: Full of desires, with heaven as their goal, (they speak words that are directed to ends) leading to new births as the result of their works, and prescribe various methods abounding in specific actions, for the attainment of pleasure and power.

simpleVersion: Krishna says those absorbed in pleasure and power, with minds pulled away by such thinking, cannot develop the steady focus needed for meditation.
explanation: Krishna explains the cost of this desire-driven mindset. When someone is preoccupied with pleasure and power, their mind can't settle into the kind of clear, resolved focus needed for deep meditation and inner steadiness.

source.sanskrit:
भोगैश्वर्यप्रसक्तानां तयापहृतचेतसाम्।

व्यवसायात्मिका बुद्धिः समाधौ न विधीयते।।2.44।।
source.transliteration:
bhogaiśwvarya-prasaktānāṁ tayāpahṛita-chetasām
vyavasāyātmikā buddhiḥ samādhau na vidhīyate
source.translation: For those who are attached to pleasure and power, whose minds are drawn away by such teachings, their determinate reason is not formed which is steadily bent on meditation and Samadhi (superconscious state).

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to rise above the scriptures' three basic qualities, stay free of opposites, remain steady, and rest in the Self.
explanation: Krishna instructs Arjuna to move beyond the surface-level concerns of ritual and reward. Instead, he should aim to stay balanced amid life's opposites, remain grounded in steady goodness, let go of constant acquiring and safeguarding, and rest in the Self.

source.sanskrit:
त्रैगुण्यविषया वेदा निस्त्रैगुण्यो भवार्जुन।

निर्द्वन्द्वो नित्यसत्त्वस्थो निर्योगक्षेम आत्मवान्।।2.45।।
source.transliteration:
trai-guṇya-viṣhayā vedā nistrai-guṇyo bhavārjuna
nirdvandvo nitya-sattva-stho niryoga-kṣhema ātmavān
source.translation: The Vedas deal with the three attributes; be thou above these three attributes. O Arjuna, free yourself from the pairs of opposites and ever remain in the quality of Sattva, freed from acquisition and preservation, and be established in the Self.

simpleVersion: Krishna says for someone who has realized the Self, scripture is about as useful as a small well beside a great flood.
explanation: Krishna uses a vivid comparison to make his point. For a person who has already realized the deeper truth of the Self, following every detail of scripture becomes almost unnecessary, much like a small reservoir loses its purpose when surrounded by a flood.

source.sanskrit:
यावानर्थ उदपाने सर्वतः संप्लुतोदके।

तावान्सर्वेषु वेदेषु ब्राह्मणस्य विजानतः।।2.46।।
source.transliteration:
yāvān artha udapāne sarvataḥ samplutodake
tāvānsarveṣhu vedeṣhu brāhmaṇasya vijānataḥ
source.translation: To the Brahmana who has known the Self, all the Vedas are of as much use as a reservoir of water would be in a place where there is a flood.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna he has a right to act, but never to the results, and shouldn't be motivated by outcomes or avoid action.
explanation: Krishna delivers one of the Gita's most famous instructions. Arjuna's responsibility is limited to doing the work itself, not to controlling or claiming its results. He should neither act purely for reward nor use that as an excuse to do nothing.
lifeLesson: Focus on doing your part well; the outcome was never fully within your control to begin with.

source.sanskrit:
कर्मण्येवाधिकारस्ते मा फलेषु कदाचन।

मा कर्मफलहेतुर्भूर्मा ते सङ्गोऽस्त्वकर्मणि।।2.47।।
source.transliteration:
karmaṇy-evādhikāras te mā phaleṣhu kadāchana
mā karma-phala-hetur bhūr mā te saṅgo ’stvakarmaṇi
source.translation: Your right is only to work, but not to its results; do not let the results of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to act established in yoga, letting go of attachment, treating success and failure equally; that balance is yoga.
explanation: Krishna defines Yoga in practical terms here: it is the ability to act with a steady, balanced mind, without clinging to attachment or being shaken by whether things succeed or fail.

source.sanskrit:
योगस्थः कुरु कर्माणि सङ्गं त्यक्त्वा धनञ्जय।

सिद्ध्यसिद्ध्योः समो भूत्वा समत्वं योग उच्यते।।2.48।।
source.transliteration:
yoga-sthaḥ kuru karmāṇi saṅgaṁ tyaktvā dhanañjaya
siddhy-asiddhyoḥ samo bhūtvā samatvaṁ yoga uchyate
source.translation: Perform action, O Arjuna, being steadfast in Yoga, abandoning attachment and balanced in success and failure; evenness of mind is called Yoga.

simpleVersion: Krishna says action alone is far less valuable than acting with steady wisdom, since those driven only by results suffer.
explanation: Krishna elevates the importance of inner wisdom over mere activity. Acting without that steady inner awareness is, he says, a lesser path, and he encourages Arjuna to root himself in wisdom rather than chase after results, which he calls a source of suffering.

source.sanskrit:
दूरेण ह्यवरं कर्म बुद्धियोगाद्धनञ्जय।

बुद्धौ शरणमन्विच्छ कृपणाः फलहेतवः।।2.49।।
source.transliteration:
dūreṇa hy-avaraṁ karma buddhi-yogād dhanañjaya
buddhau śharaṇam anvichchha kṛipaṇāḥ phala-hetavaḥ
source.translation: Far lower than the Yoga of wisdom is action, O Arjuna. Seek thou refuge in wisdom; wretched are those whose motive is the fruit.

simpleVersion: Krishna says a person acting with steady wisdom rises above good and bad deeds alike; Arjuna should aim for this skillful way of acting.
explanation: Krishna explains a benefit of acting with wisdom: it allows a person to move beyond being bound by either their good or bad actions. He calls this skillful, balanced way of acting real Yoga.

source.sanskrit:
बुद्धियुक्तो जहातीह उभे सुकृतदुष्कृते।

तस्माद्योगाय युज्यस्व योगः कर्मसु कौशलम्।।2.50।।
source.transliteration:
buddhi-yukto jahātīha ubhe sukṛita-duṣhkṛite
tasmād yogāya yujyasva yogaḥ karmasu kauśhalam
source.translation: Endowed with wisdom and evenness of mind, one casts off in this life both good and evil deeds; therefore, devote yourself to Yoga; Yoga is skill in action.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the wise, letting go of the results of their actions and freed from rebirth's cycle, reach a state free of suffering.
explanation: Krishna describes where this path leads. By releasing their grip on outcomes, wise people are eventually freed from repeated cycles of birth, arriving at a state untouched by suffering or harm.

source.sanskrit:
कर्मजं बुद्धियुक्ता हि फलं त्यक्त्वा मनीषिणः।

जन्मबन्धविनिर्मुक्ताः पदं गच्छन्त्यनामयम्।।2.51।।
source.transliteration:
karma-jaṁ buddhi-yuktā hi phalaṁ tyaktvā manīṣhiṇaḥ
janma-bandha-vinirmuktāḥ padaṁ gachchhanty-anāmayam
source.translation: The wise, possessing knowledge, having abandoned the fruits of their actions, and being freed from the bonds of birth, go to the place which is beyond all evil.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that once his mind moves past confusion, he will become indifferent to everything he has heard or has yet to hear.
explanation: Krishna reassures Arjuna about the clarity waiting ahead. Once his intellect works through the current confusion, he'll reach a place where even scriptural debates and accumulated knowledge lose their grip on him.

source.sanskrit:
यदा ते मोहकलिलं बुद्धिर्व्यतितरिष्यति।

तदा गन्तासि निर्वेदं श्रोतव्यस्य श्रुतस्य च।।2.52।।
source.transliteration:
yadā te moha-kalilaṁ buddhir vyatitariṣhyati
tadā gantāsi nirvedaṁ śhrotavyasya śhrutasya cha
source.translation: When your intellect passes beyond the mire of delusion, then you will attain indifference to what has been heard and what has yet to be heard.

simpleVersion: Krishna says once Arjuna's mind stops being pulled around by conflicting scriptures and becomes steady and unshaken, he will attain true inner union.
explanation: Krishna describes the final stage of this inner steadiness: when the mind, once confused by competing teachings, finally settles into an unwavering, focused state, that stillness itself is what leads to Self-realization.

source.sanskrit:
श्रुतिविप्रतिपन्ना ते यदा स्थास्यति निश्चला।

समाधावचला बुद्धिस्तदा योगमवाप्स्यसि।।2.53।।
source.transliteration:
śhruti-vipratipannā te yadā sthāsyati niśhchalā
samādhāv-achalā buddhis tadā yogam avāpsyasi
source.translation: When your intellect, which is perplexed by the Vedic texts you have read, stands immovable and steady in the Self, then you will attain Self-realization.

simpleVersion: Arjuna asks Krishna how a person of steady wisdom, absorbed in deep inner stillness, actually speaks, sits, and moves through the world.
explanation: Curious and engaged now, Arjuna asks a very practical question. He wants to know what a person with steady, unshaken wisdom actually looks like in daily life, how they talk, sit, and act.

source.sanskrit:
अर्जुन उवाच

स्थितप्रज्ञस्य का भाषा समाधिस्थस्य केशव।

स्थितधीः किं प्रभाषेत किमासीत व्रजेत किम्।।2.54।।
source.transliteration:
arjuna uvācha
sthita-prajñasya kā bhāṣhā samādhi-sthasya keśhava
sthita-dhīḥ kiṁ prabhāṣheta kim āsīta vrajeta kim
source.translation: Arjuna said, "O Krishna, what is the description of one who has steady wisdom and is merged in the superconscious state? How does one of steady wisdom speak, how do they sit, and how do they walk?"

simpleVersion: Krishna says a person is called steady in wisdom when they let go of every mental desire and find contentment in the Self alone.
explanation: Krishna begins to answer Arjuna's question directly. He defines a person of steady wisdom as someone who has released all mental cravings and finds complete satisfaction from within, rather than from anything outside.

source.sanskrit:
श्री भगवानुवाच

प्रजहाति यदा कामान् सर्वान् पार्थ मनोगतान्।

आत्मन्येवात्मना तुष्टः स्थितप्रज्ञस्तदोच्यते।।2.55।।
source.transliteration:
śhrī bhagavān uvācha
prajahāti yadā kāmān sarvān pārtha mano-gatān
ātmany-evātmanā tuṣhṭaḥ sthita-prajñas tadochyate
source.translation: The Blessed Lord said, "When a man completely casts off, O Arjuna, all the desires of the mind and is satisfied in the Self by the Self, then he is said to be one of steady wisdom."

simpleVersion: Krishna describes the steady sage as someone unshaken by hardship, uninterested in chasing pleasure, and free from attachment, fear, and anger.
explanation: Krishna continues the description. This person remains calm when facing difficulty, doesn't crave pleasure, and has moved beyond the grip of attachment, fear, and anger, qualities most people struggle with constantly.

source.sanskrit:
दुःखेष्वनुद्विग्नमनाः सुखेषु विगतस्पृहः।

वीतरागभयक्रोधः स्थितधीर्मुनिरुच्यते।।2.56।।
source.transliteration:
duḥkheṣhv-anudvigna-manāḥ sukheṣhu vigata-spṛihaḥ
vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhaḥ sthita-dhīr munir uchyate
source.translation: He whose mind is not shaken by adversity, who does not long for pleasures, and is free from attachment, fear, and anger, is called a sage of steady wisdom.
