simpleVersion: Krishna says someone unattached everywhere, who neither celebrates good fortune nor resents bad, has firmly established wisdom.
explanation: Krishna adds another marker of steady wisdom: emotional balance in the face of both good and bad outcomes. This person doesn't get swept up in either happiness or resentment when life brings favorable or unfavorable events.

source.sanskrit:
यः सर्वत्रानभिस्नेहस्तत्तत्प्राप्य शुभाशुभम्।

नाभिनन्दति न द्वेष्टि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.57।।
source.transliteration:
yaḥ sarvatrānabhisnehas tat tat prāpya śhubhāśhubham
nābhinandati na dveṣhṭi tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: He who is everywhere without attachment, upon encountering anything good or bad, neither rejoices nor hastens; his wisdom is firm.

simpleVersion: Just as a tortoise pulls all its limbs inward, the wise person withdraws their senses from external objects, and that's when their wisdom becomes steady.
explanation: Krishna offers another memorable image: the tortoise drawing its limbs into its shell. In the same way, a person of steady wisdom can pull their senses back from external distractions whenever needed, keeping their inner focus intact.

source.sanskrit:
यदा संहरते चायं कूर्मोऽङ्गानीव सर्वशः।

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.58।।
source.transliteration:
yadā sanharate chāyaṁ kūrmo ’ṅgānīva sarvaśhaḥ
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyas tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: When, like the tortoise which withdraws all its limbs on all sides, he withdraws his senses from the sense-objects, then his wisdom becomes steady.

simpleVersion: Even when a person stops indulging the senses, some longing can remain, but that longing too fades once they experience something greater.
explanation: Krishna notes a subtlety: simply avoiding sense objects doesn't fully remove the underlying craving for them. That craving only truly dissolves once a person experiences the deeper reality of the Self.

source.sanskrit:
विषया विनिवर्तन्ते निराहारस्य देहिनः।

रसवर्जं रसोऽप्यस्य परं दृष्ट्वा निवर्तते।।2.59।।
source.transliteration:
viṣhayā vinivartante nirāhārasya dehinaḥ
rasa-varjaṁ raso ’pyasya paraṁ dṛiṣhṭvā nivartate
source.translation: The objects of the senses turn away from the abstinent man, leaving the longing behind; but his longing also turns away upon seeing the Supreme.

simpleVersion: Krishna warns that even a wise person who is trying hard can have their mind forcefully swept away by the restless senses.
explanation: Krishna gives an honest warning here. Even someone sincerely working toward self-control isn't immune; the senses are powerful enough that they can still overwhelm and drag away the mind despite one's best efforts.

source.sanskrit:
यततो ह्यपि कौन्तेय पुरुषस्य विपश्चितः।

इन्द्रियाणि प्रमाथीनि हरन्ति प्रसभं मनः।।2.60।।
source.transliteration:
yatato hyapi kaunteya puruṣhasya vipaśhchitaḥ
indriyāṇi pramāthīni haranti prasabhaṁ manaḥ
source.translation: The turbulent senses, O Arjuna, can violently carry away the mind of a wise person, even though they are striving to control them.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna to bring all the senses under control and sit focused on Him, since wisdom is steady for one whose senses are mastered.
explanation: Krishna offers the solution to the previous verse's warning. He instructs Arjuna to actively restrain his senses and stay centered on Him. This kind of mastery over the senses is what keeps wisdom firm and unshaken.

source.sanskrit:
तानि सर्वाणि संयम्य युक्त आसीत मत्परः।

वशे हि यस्येन्द्रियाणि तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.61।।
source.transliteration:
tāni sarvāṇi sanyamya yukta āsīta mat-paraḥ
vaśhe hi yasyendriyāṇi tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: Having restrained them all, he should sit steadfast, intent on Me; his wisdom is steady whose senses are under control.

simpleVersion: Krishna explains that dwelling on objects creates attachment to them, attachment gives rise to desire, and desire, when blocked, turns into anger.
explanation: Krishna lays out a cause-and-effect chain that begins with something as ordinary as thinking about an object. That simple act of dwelling on something can quietly grow into attachment, then desire, and eventually anger.
lifeLesson: Notice where a chain reaction of frustration actually starts; often it traces back to simply dwelling too long on something.

source.sanskrit:
ध्यायतो विषयान्पुंसः सङ्गस्तेषूपजायते।

सङ्गात् संजायते कामः कामात्क्रोधोऽभिजायते।।2.62।।
source.transliteration:
dhyāyato viṣhayān puṁsaḥ saṅgas teṣhūpajāyate
saṅgāt sañjāyate kāmaḥ kāmāt krodho ’bhijāyate
source.translation: When one thinks of objects, attachment to them arises; from attachment, desire is born; from desire, anger arises.

simpleVersion: Krishna continues the chain: anger causes confusion, confusion causes memory to fail, and losing memory destroys judgment, which then ruins a person entirely.
explanation: Krishna finishes the chain of decline he began in the previous verse. Anger clouds clear thinking, clouded thinking erodes memory, and once memory and judgment break down, a person is left without any real direction at all.

source.sanskrit:
क्रोधाद्भवति संमोहः संमोहात्स्मृतिविभ्रमः।

स्मृतिभ्रंशाद् बुद्धिनाशो बुद्धिनाशात्प्रणश्यति।।2.63।।
source.transliteration:
krodhād bhavati sammohaḥ sammohāt smṛiti-vibhramaḥ
smṛiti-bhranśhād buddhi-nāśho buddhi-nāśhāt praṇaśhyati
source.translation: Anger leads to delusion, which causes loss of memory; this, in turn, leads to the destruction of discrimination, resulting in destruction.

simpleVersion: Krishna says a self-controlled person, moving through the world with restrained senses and free from attraction and aversion, attains genuine inner peace.
explanation: Krishna offers the counterpoint to the destructive chain reaction. A person who engages with the world using disciplined senses, without being pulled by likes and dislikes, arrives instead at real peace of mind.

source.sanskrit:
रागद्वेषवियुक्तैस्तु विषयानिन्द्रियैश्चरन्।

आत्मवश्यैर्विधेयात्मा प्रसादमधिगच्छति।।2.64।।
source.transliteration:
rāga-dveṣha-viyuktais tu viṣhayān indriyaiśh charan
ātma-vaśhyair-vidheyātmā prasādam adhigachchhati
source.translation: But the self-controlled man, moving among objects with the senses restrained and free from attraction and repulsion, attains peace.

simpleVersion: Krishna says in that state of peace, all suffering ends, since the mind of someone truly tranquil quickly becomes steady and clear.
explanation: Krishna describes the reward of that hard-won peace: once it's reached, sorrow simply dissolves, and a tranquil mind naturally settles into steadiness without much further effort.

source.sanskrit:
प्रसादे सर्वदुःखानां हानिरस्योपजायते।

प्रसन्नचेतसो ह्याशु बुद्धिः पर्यवतिष्ठते।।2.65।।
source.transliteration:
prasāde sarva-duḥkhānāṁ hānir asyopajāyate
prasanna-chetaso hyāśhu buddhiḥ paryavatiṣhṭhate
source.translation: In that peace, all pains are destroyed; for the intellect of the tranquil-minded soon becomes steady.

simpleVersion: Krishna says a scattered, undisciplined mind has no real wisdom or focus, and without peace, there can be no true happiness.
explanation: Krishna underlines why inner discipline matters so much. Without a settled mind, real understanding isn't possible, and without that understanding, there's no lasting peace, and without peace, genuine happiness simply can't exist.

source.sanskrit:
नास्ति बुद्धिरयुक्तस्य न चायुक्तस्य भावना।

न चाभावयतः शान्तिरशान्तस्य कुतः सुखम्।।2.66।।
source.transliteration:
nāsti buddhir-ayuktasya na chāyuktasya bhāvanā
na chābhāvayataḥ śhāntir aśhāntasya kutaḥ sukham
source.translation: There is no knowledge of the Self for the unsteady, and no meditation is possible for the unsteady, and no peace for the unmeditative, and how can there be happiness for one who has no peace?

simpleVersion: Krishna says the mind following the wandering senses drags away a person's judgment, the way wind drags a boat off course.
explanation: Krishna offers a vivid sailing metaphor. Just as a strong wind can push a boat far off its intended path, a mind that keeps chasing after the senses can just as easily carry away a person's clear judgment.

source.sanskrit:
इन्द्रियाणां हि चरतां यन्मनोऽनुविधीयते।

तदस्य हरति प्रज्ञां वायुर्नावमिवाम्भसि।।2.67।।
source.transliteration:
indriyāṇāṁ hi charatāṁ yan mano ’nuvidhīyate
tadasya harati prajñāṁ vāyur nāvam ivāmbhasi
source.translation: For the mind, which follows in the wake of the wandering senses, carries away his discrimination, as the wind carries away a boat on the waters.

simpleVersion: Krishna tells Arjuna that whoever keeps their senses completely restrained from sense objects has truly steady wisdom.
explanation: Krishna restates the core principle clearly: real, unshakeable wisdom belongs to the person who has learned to fully hold their senses back from constantly chasing after external objects.

source.sanskrit:
तस्माद्यस्य महाबाहो निगृहीतानि सर्वशः।

इन्द्रियाणीन्द्रियार्थेभ्यस्तस्य प्रज्ञा प्रतिष्ठिता।।2.68।।
source.transliteration:
tasmād yasya mahā-bāho nigṛihītāni sarvaśhaḥ
indriyāṇīndriyārthebhyas tasya prajñā pratiṣhṭhitā
source.translation: Therefore, O mighty-armed Arjuna, his knowledge is steady whose senses are completely restrained from sense objects.

simpleVersion: Krishna says what feels like night to most is when the disciplined person is awake, and what others wake to is night to the wise.
explanation: Krishna points to a striking reversal in perspective. What ordinary people are absorbed in during their waking lives is, in a sense, unseen and dark to the wise, while the deeper reality the wise are attuned to remains hidden from everyone else.

source.sanskrit:
या निशा सर्वभूतानां तस्यां जागर्ति संयमी।

यस्यां जाग्रति भूतानि सा निशा पश्यतो मुनेः।।2.69।।
source.transliteration:
yā niśhā sarva-bhūtānāṁ tasyāṁ jāgarti sanyamī
yasyāṁ jāgrati bhūtāni sā niśhā paśhyato muneḥ
source.translation: That which is night to all beings, in that the self-controlled man is awake; when all beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees.

simpleVersion: Krishna compares a peaceful person to the ocean, staying full and unmoved as rivers flow in; only someone free of craving finds peace.
explanation: Krishna uses the image of the ocean absorbing countless rivers without ever overflowing or being disturbed. In the same way, a peaceful person can let all desires arrive without being shaken, unlike someone constantly chasing after them.

source.sanskrit:
आपूर्यमाणमचलप्रतिष्ठं

समुद्रमापः प्रविशन्ति यद्वत्।

तद्वत्कामा यं प्रविशन्ति सर्वे

स शान्तिमाप्नोति न कामकामी।।2.70।।
source.transliteration:
āpūryamāṇam achala-pratiṣhṭhaṁ
samudram āpaḥ praviśhanti yadvat
tadvat kāmā yaṁ praviśhanti sarve
sa śhāntim āpnoti na kāma-kāmī
source.translation: He attains peace into whom all desires enter, just as waters enter the ocean which, filled from all sides, remains unmoved; but not the man who is full of desires.

simpleVersion: Krishna says the person who lets go of all desires, moving through life without craving, ownership, or ego, finds true peace.
explanation: Krishna offers a summary description of what leads to lasting peace: releasing personal desires, giving up the sense of owning things, and letting go of ego, all working together to bring someone to a genuinely peaceful state.

source.sanskrit:
विहाय कामान्यः सर्वान्पुमांश्चरति निःस्पृहः।

निर्ममो निरहंकारः स शांतिमधिगच्छति।।2.71।।
source.transliteration:
vihāya kāmān yaḥ sarvān pumānśh charati niḥspṛihaḥ
nirmamo nirahankāraḥ sa śhāntim adhigachchhati
source.translation: That person attains peace who, abandoning all desires, moves about without longing, without the sense of ownership, and without egoism.

simpleVersion: Krishna closes: this eternal, divine state, once reached, ends confusion for good, even at the moment of death.
explanation: Krishna concludes his teaching for this chapter. He calls the state he has been describing the highest, divine condition, one that, once attained, removes all confusion permanently, allowing a person to merge fully with the ultimate reality even in their final moment.

source.sanskrit:
एषा ब्राह्मी स्थितिः पार्थ नैनां प्राप्य विमुह्यति।

स्थित्वाऽस्यामन्तकालेऽपि ब्रह्मनिर्वाणमृच्छति।।2.72।।
source.transliteration:
eṣhā brāhmī sthitiḥ pārtha naināṁ prāpya vimuhyati
sthitvāsyām anta-kāle ’pi brahma-nirvāṇam ṛichchhati
source.translation: O son of Pritha, this is the eternal state, the Brahmic seat. Attaining this, one is not deluded. Being established in it, one attains oneness with Brahman even at the end of life.
